summary: Specifies how to handle DHCPv4 options that show up more than once in a message, which happens when an option is longer than the 255-byte limit or is split to use option overloading. It updates RFC 2131.

eli5.summary: A DHCP option fits only so many characters, like a text message limit. This explains how to split a long one over several pieces and glue them back.

questions: how do dhcp long options work
what is the dhcp option size limit
how to encode dhcp options longer than 255 bytes
how to split dhcp options longer than 255 bytes
subtitle: How to split a DHCPv4 option longer than 255 bytes into pieces and glue it back together.

tldr.problem: A DHCPv4 option has a one-byte length, so it holds at most 255 bytes, and options also have to fit into the limited space of the option fields in a packet.
tldr.mechanism: An option may be split into several instances with the same option code, stored in order in an aggregate option buffer; the receiver concatenates all instances of the same code into one option before processing.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 2131 by replacing its 'options may appear only once' text with clear concatenation rules, but senders must be careful because many deployed agents do not implement concatenation.

today: RFC 3396 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2002. It updates RFC 2131, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Options Need Splitting
sections.content:
DHCP carries configuration data in options. Each option is a one-byte type code, a one-byte length, and a buffer of between zero and 255 bytes. Some options are useful at more than 255 bytes, and a sender may also need to break an option up to fit it into the space it has.

This document updates RFC 2131 by clarifying the option concatenation rules of its section 4.1. The sentence there that says options may appear only once, unless otherwise specified, is to be considered deleted. RFC 2131 said that repeated options should be concatenated but did not say in what order; this RFC supplies the order.
sections.eli5: Each option is a short note with a size limit. Sometimes the note is too long, so this RFC says how to cut it up and in what order to read the pieces.

sections.title: Agents and Option Overload
sections.content:
The RFC uses a few terms. A DHCP protocol agent is any client, server or relay agent that sends or receives DHCP packets. The encoding agent composes a packet to send; the decoding agent processes one it received.

DHCP packets are based on the BOOTP format, which has three fields that can hold options: the optional parameters field, the sname field and the filename field. The Overload option from RFC 2132 says which of these are actually used to store options in a given message.
sections.eli5: The sender packs the message and the receiver unpacks it. A packet has three places where notes can be stored, and a special note says which places are in use.

sections.title: When Splitting Is Allowed
sections.content:
Splitting is needed in two cases. First, when an option value is longer than 255 bytes, the encoding agent MUST follow the algorithm in this RFC. Second, when the current output buffer has room for only part of an option and another buffer has room for the rest, the agent MUST either use this algorithm or not send the option at all.

On the receiving side, any agent that gets more than one instance of an option of the same type MUST concatenate them. No restrictions apply to concatenation on receipt.

Many deployed DHCP agents do not implement concatenation. An agent SHOULD NOT split an option unless it has no choice or knows its peer can handle split options. A peer is assumed to cope if it has provided or requested at least one concatenation-requiring option, or if an administrator has configured the agent to assume so.

A concatenation-requiring option is one whose specification explicitly requires this document's mechanism. An implementation that supports any such option MUST be able to concatenate received options of every kind.
sections.eli5: You should only cut a note into pieces if you must, or if you know the reader can glue them back. Some readers cannot, so be careful.

sections.title: The Aggregate Option Buffer and Encoding Rules
sections.content:
To describe splitting across the three option fields, the RFC defines a logical aggregate option buffer. It is the optional parameters field, then the file field, then the sname field, in that order. This is not the physical order of the fields in the packet. An option MUST NOT cross a boundary between the fields. If the encoding agent does not use the sname or file field, that field is not part of the aggregate.

When encoding, an option can be split on any octet boundary, and no piece may contain more than 255 octets. The pieces MUST be stored in sequence: first piece first, then the second, and so on. A three-way split could therefore put the first part in the optional parameters field, the second in the file field and the third in the sname field. Each piece is stored like a normal variable-length option, all pieces carry the same option code, and their lengths add up to the total length of the option data. The encoder MUST NOT attach any meaning to where the split falls.
sections.eli5: Imagine three drawers read in a fixed order. You put piece one in the first drawer, piece two in the next, and so on, and every piece has the same label.

sections.title: Decoding Agent Behavior
sections.content:
When a decoding agent scans the option buffer and finds two or more options with the same code, it MUST treat them as split portions of one option. It reassembles them in the order described for the encoder and treats the result as a single object. It MUST NOT handle each portion as a separate option.

Because the split point has no semantic meaning, the receiver must not read anything into it. The decoder should also deal with any machine-specific alignment issues when it uses the value, since the encoder is not required to align options in any particular way.
sections.eli5: The reader sees several pieces with the same label and sticks them together in order. It does not matter where the cuts were.

sections.title: Worked Example: Bootfile Name
sections.content: The RFC uses Bootfile name (option code 67) with the value /diskless/foo. Unsplit, it is one option with code 67 and length 13. If the encoder must split it, it can send two options: code 67 with length 7 holding /diskle, followed by code 67 with length 6 holding ss/foo. The decoder joins them back into /diskless/foo.
sections.eli5: A word is cut into two parts, both labeled the same, and the reader joins them to get the whole word.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it raises no new security issues and points to section 7 of RFC 2131 and to RFC 3118 for the existing exposures in DHCP.

It adds one warning: the authentication option itself can be split. Implementations must therefore take care when setting the authentication field to zero before generating or verifying the MAC, because that field may span several options.
sections.eli5: Splitting adds no new danger, but if a secret signature is cut into pieces, you must be careful to handle all the pieces when you check it.
